blocks.text: 1. Validation Loops

blocks.alt: Validation data runs through a forward pass only, forming the validation loop

blocks.text: Training Loops, the previous topic, covered the four core steps repeated every iteration during training. Validation Loops take a closer look at the validation pass already introduced there, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
A validation loop measures performance on data the network never trains on, a genuinely essential companion process to the training loop already covered in the previous topic.
2. Recapping The Purpose Of Validation Data

This connects back to validation data, already covered throughout this course. It is held out from training entirely, used only to measure genuine generalization, never contributing directly to any weight update.
This is exactly the data a validation loop processes, already covered, giving an honest, unbiased read on how well the network performs on examples it has genuinely never seen during training.

blocks.text: 3. The Key Difference From A Training Loop

blocks.alt: A training loop does forward and backward while a validation loop does forward only

blocks.text: This connects back to the four core steps already covered in Training Loops. A validation loop runs the forward pass and computes loss, exactly as covered there, using the exact same computations.
It genuinely skips the backward pass and the weight update entirely, the two steps already covered as the third and fourth of the four core steps in that earlier topic.
4. Why Skipping The Backward Pass Genuinely Matters

This connects back to the exact purpose of validation data, already covered in this topic. The network must never genuinely learn from validation data, or its held-out status, already covered, would be violated entirely.
Running a backward pass and update would defeat that entire purpose, since the network would then have genuinely trained on the exact data meant to measure its unbiased generalization performance.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: Accidentally running a backward pass or weight update during validation, already covered in this topic, is a genuinely serious real bug. It silently corrupts the validation loss into an overly optimistic, misleading number.

blocks.text: 5. Switching Into Evaluation Mode

blocks.alt: The model gets set to evaluation mode

blocks.text: This connects back to Dropout and Batch Normalization, already covered in earlier modules. The network must be genuinely switched into evaluation mode before the validation loop begins, the direct counterpart to training mode already covered in Training Loops.

This ensures those techniques' own inference-time behavior, already covered, actually applies, meaning Dropout stops randomly disabling neurons and Batch Normalization uses its running average statistics instead of batch statistics.
6. No Gradient Tracking Needed

blocks.alt: A validation loop tracks no gradients

blocks.text: A genuinely important computational optimization follows. Since no backward pass happens, already covered in this topic, gradients never need to be tracked at all throughout the entire validation loop.

This genuinely saves memory and computation during the entire validation pass, since the bookkeeping normally required to support Backpropagation, already covered in its own topic, becomes entirely unnecessary here.
7. When Validation Loops Run Within Training

blocks.alt: Each epoch runs a validation loop

blocks.text: This connects back to the outer loop, already covered in Training Loops. A validation loop typically runs once per epoch, right after that epoch's training iterations finish, nested inside the same outer loop.
This produces exactly the validation loss already covered as one of the two Learning Curves lines, confirming the direct, concrete link between this topic and both Training Loops and Learning Curves.

blocks.text: 8. The Distinction From A Final Test Set

blocks.alt: The validation set is used during training while the test set is used only at the end

blocks.text: A genuinely important, related distinction applies here too. This connects back to validation data being used repeatedly throughout training, already covered, checked at the end of every single epoch.

A genuinely separate test set gets used only once, at the genuinely very end, after all training and hyperparameter decisions are already finalized, avoiding the kind of repeated exposure that validation data genuinely receives.
9. Recognizing Why A Genuinely Correct Validation Loop Matters
Producing trustworthy Learning Curves, already covered, is a direct case where a validation loop with a bug, like accidentally updating weights, would genuinely corrupt those curves entirely.

Deciding when to apply Early Stopping, already covered, is another genuine case where that technique genuinely depends entirely on accurate, uncorrupted validation loss values, already covered throughout this topic.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely complete validation loop, run once after each training epoch, using the same network but explicitly skipping the backward pass and weight update.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def validation_loop(X_val, y_val, weights, batch_size=32):
    total_loss = 0.0
    num_batches = 0

    for start in range(0, len(X_val), batch_size):  # the inner loop structure, already covered in Training Loops
        X_batch = X_val[start:start + batch_size]
        y_batch = y_val[start:start + batch_size]

        predictions = X_batch @ weights   # forward pass only, already covered as the key difference in this topic
        errors = predictions - y_batch
        loss = np.mean(errors ** 2)       # compute loss, already covered
        # No backward pass, no weight update here at all, already covered as this topic's own key difference

        total_loss += loss
        num_batches += 1

    return total_loss / num_batches

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X_val = rng.normal(size=(64, 3))
true_weights = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5])
y_val = X_val @ true_weights + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=64)
current_weights = np.array([1.8, -0.9, 0.4])  # a partially trained model

val_loss = validation_loop(X_val, y_val, current_weights)
print(f"Validation loss: {val_loss:.4f}")
print("This value contributes directly to the validation curve already covered in Learning Curves")

blocks.content: Running this example computes a genuine validation loss without ever touching the weights, exactly the read-only measurement already covered as this topic's own defining characteristic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A validation loop measures performance on data the network never trains on.
It runs the forward pass and computes loss, but skips the backward pass and weight update entirely.
Skipping the backward pass preserves validation data's unbiased, held-out status.
The network must be switched into evaluation mode so Dropout and Batch Normalization behave correctly.
No gradient tracking is needed, saving memory and computation.
It typically runs once per epoch, right after that epoch's training iterations finish.
A separate test set, used only once at the very end, is distinct from validation data's repeated use.
Correct validation loops are essential for trustworthy Learning Curves and correct Early Stopping decisions.
